result.goal: Compare two mechanisms for a single-process JSON checkpoint and produce a conditional, source-grounded recommendation with independent review.
result.baseline: A: directly truncate and rewrite the checkpoint file. B: write complete JSON to a temporary file on the destination filesystem, close it, then publish with os.replace.
constraints: Purpose is design; no efficacy experiment or performance claim.
Two-candidate exception: the requirements explicitly limit the decision to these two real mechanisms; additional methods would expand the question.
Use only the fixture requirements and decisive Python os.replace and Linux rename(2) primary passages.
Python evidence: https://docs.python.org/3/library/os.html#os.replace, decisive passage at lines 1833–1836 confirms atomic rename on success and possible cross-filesystem failure.
Linux evidence pending: https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/rename.2.html, DESCRIPTION replacement semantics and ERRORS EXDEV.
Do not treat atomic visibility as a power-loss durability guarantee; the named sources cannot establish a complete durability protocol.

Examples are illustrative reasoning, not measured outcomes; retain retrieval failures and unknowns.

criteria.title: Conditional mechanism choice
criteria.acceptance: Compare A and B and condition the recommendation on preserving a complete checkpoint during interrupted updates versus accepting checkpoint loss for simpler writes. Explain both mechanisms without claiming measured effectiveness.

criteria.title: Atomic publication scope
criteria.acceptance: Ground successful replacement semantics in the decisive Python and Linux passages. Distinguish publication of a completed temporary file from atomicity of its preceding writes; explain that existing open descriptors can retain the old file.

criteria.title: Durability boundary
criteria.acceptance: Separate atomic pathname visibility from persistence after power loss or system crash. State that durability is unmeasured and a complete synchronization protocol is not established by these passages.

criteria.title: Filesystem constraint
criteria.acceptance: Verify Linux EXDEV and Python's cross-filesystem warning; require the temporary file on the destination filesystem, preferably in its directory. Do not present a cross-filesystem copy fallback as atomic replacement.

criteria.title: Independent evidence review
criteria.acceptance: An independent reviewer checks the final explanation against the original decisive passages and R1–R4, retaining unsupported claims and source gaps as unresolved. Completion requires the Linux source gap to be closed.

result.complexity_baseline: A uses one destination write sequence. B adds temporary-file lifecycle and a replacement operation. Compare these structural costs qualitatively; no timing or reliability measurement.

criteria.acceptance: Compare A and B and condition the recommendation on preserving a complete checkpoint during interrupted updates versus accepting checkpoint loss for simpler writes. Explain both mechanisms without claiming measured effectiveness.

criteria.title: Atomic publication scope

criteria.title: Durability boundary

claims.statement: B separates preparation from publication: conditional on complete JSON preparation and successful replacement, the destination pathname publishes the prepared file. Preceding temporary-file writes remain separate operations.

limitations: Actual interruption behavior is unmeasured. Same-mount placement is necessary for the stated Linux rename mechanism but does not guarantee success.

plan.reason: Design plan frozen. Requirements and evaluation contract read; Python os.replace passage verified. Linux rename(2) retrieval failed through web access and curl DNS resolution; its decisive passages remain a required evidence gap before completion.
plan.goal: Compare two mechanisms for a single-process JSON checkpoint and produce a conditional, source-grounded recommendation with independent review.
plan.baseline: A: directly truncate and rewrite the checkpoint file. B: write complete JSON to a temporary file on the destination filesystem, close it, then publish with os.replace.
constraints: Purpose is design; no efficacy experiment or performance claim.
Two-candidate exception: the requirements explicitly limit the decision to these two real mechanisms; additional methods would expand the question.
Use only the fixture requirements and decisive Python os.replace and Linux rename(2) primary passages.
Python evidence: https://docs.python.org/3/library/os.html#os.replace, decisive passage at lines 1833–1836 confirms atomic rename on success and possible cross-filesystem failure.
Linux evidence pending: https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/rename.2.html, DESCRIPTION replacement semantics and ERRORS EXDEV.
Do not treat atomic visibility as a power-loss durability guarantee; the named sources cannot establish a complete durability protocol.
No checks executed, files modified, packages installed, memory written, commits or deployments.
Examples are illustrative reasoning, not measured outcomes; retain retrieval failures and unknowns.

criteria.title: Conditional mechanism choice
criteria.acceptance: Compare A and B and condition the recommendation on preserving a complete checkpoint during interrupted updates versus accepting checkpoint loss for simpler writes. Explain both mechanisms without claiming measured effectiveness.

criteria.title: Atomic publication scope
criteria.acceptance: Ground successful replacement semantics in the decisive Python and Linux passages. Distinguish publication of a completed temporary file from atomicity of its preceding writes; explain that existing open descriptors can retain the old file.

criteria.title: Durability boundary
criteria.acceptance: Separate atomic pathname visibility from persistence after power loss or system crash. State that durability is unmeasured and a complete synchronization protocol is not established by these passages.

criteria.title: Filesystem constraint
criteria.acceptance: Verify Linux EXDEV and Python's cross-filesystem warning; require the temporary file on the destination filesystem, preferably in its directory. Do not present a cross-filesystem copy fallback as atomic replacement.

criteria.title: Independent evidence review
criteria.acceptance: An independent reviewer checks the final explanation against the original decisive passages and R1–R4, retaining unsupported claims and source gaps as unresolved. Completion requires the Linux source gap to be closed.

plan.complexity_baseline: A uses one destination write sequence. B adds temporary-file lifecycle and a replacement operation. Compare these structural costs qualitatively; no timing or reliability measurement.

checks.reason: The proposal explains A's direct truncating rewrite and B's complete temporary-file preparation followed by replacement. It conditionally prefers B when preserving a complete checkpoint during interrupted updates matters, and A when checkpoint loss is acceptable and fewer lifecycle steps are preferred. Python os.replace documents atomic renaming on success; indexed original Linux DESCRIPTION supports atomic destination replacement. reader_guide.purpose: Prefer B when an interrupted update must preserve a complete checkpoint, conditional on complete preparation and successful replacement on the destination mount. A remains reasonable when checkpoint loss is acceptable and fewer lifecycle steps are preferred. This provisional design conclusion helps a developer choose between the two specified JSON checkpoint mechanisms; independent review remains pending.
reader_guide.scope: One single-process JSON checkpoint, one writer, an existing complete checkpoint, a distinct temporary file and no subsequent mutation. Compare A: direct truncating rewrite, with B: complete temporary-file preparation, closure and os.replace. The saved outputs contain zero experiments, metrics, experiment receipts or independent grades; there are no measured results to reuse.
reader_guide.takeaway: B separates preparation from publication. Successful renaming is documented as atomic in [Python os.replace](https://docs.python.org/3/library/os.html#os.replace). [Linux rename(2)](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/rename.2.html), DESCRIPTION, documents replacement without an interval where the destination pathname is missing. This concerns pathname visibility, not persistence after power loss. Complete-JSON publication follows conditionally from preparing complete JSON before replacement; its advantage over A is mechanism reasoning, not a measured interruption result.
reader_guide.walkthrough: Concrete with/without example, explicitly unmeasured: checkpoint.json initially contains {"step":10}; the intended update is {"step":11}. Without separate publication (A), truncate checkpoint.json and write the update directly. Interruption after truncation can leave an empty file; interruption during writing can leave incomplete JSON such as {"step":. These are hypothetical states derived from the specified mechanism, not observed failures. With separate publication (B), write {"step":11} completely into a distinct checkpoint.tmp beside checkpoint.json and close it. During this preparation, the existing checkpoint remains separate. Only then call os.replace(checkpoint.tmp, checkpoint.json). Conditional on success, pathname lookup reaches the prepared file; already-open readers can retain the old file, an inference from pathname replacement semantics. Figure F1 compares the preparation paths; F2 enlarges F1's Publish component to show the publication boundary and placement constraint. Linux rename(2), ERRORS EXDEV, requires the same mounted filesystem, even when different mounts expose the same filesystem. Prefer the destination directory for the temporary file; placement alone does not guarantee success. Treat replacement errors as failures; a cross-filesystem copy fallback has no established atomic-publication guarantee here. No code or checks were executed.
reader_guide.glossary: Checkpoint: saved JSON state used to resume work. Preparation: producing the complete next JSON file before publication. Publication: changing which file the checkpoint pathname names. Atomic pathname visibility: successful replacement presents the pathname change as one operation; preceding writes remain separate. Durability: persistence after power loss or system crash, which is unknown here. Mount: the filesystem attachment boundary relevant to Linux EXDEV. Open descriptor: an existing reference to an opened file that pathname replacement need not redirect.
reader_guide.limitations: This is a source-based design comparison, with no tested implementation or empirical dataset. Actual interruption outcomes, failure frequencies, latency, power-loss persistence and filesystem-specific effects are unmeasured. File closure and atomic replacement do not establish a complete durability protocol from the two named passages. Saved Python transport receipts record retrieval, not scientific validation. Saved Linux receipts remain unavailable after timeouts; direct web access in this unit also failed with Internal Error, while indexed text from the original page supplied decisive DESCRIPTION and EXDEV passages. Indexed reading does not replace those failed parent-owned receipts. Independent review remains pending, with no grades or acceptance supplied. Both figures are unmeasured illustrations, not measurement artifacts; their rendering has not been checked.

plan.goal: Compare two mechanisms for a single-process JSON checkpoint and produce a conditional, source-grounded recommendation with independent review.
plan.baseline: A: directly truncate and rewrite the checkpoint file. B: write complete JSON to a temporary file on the destination filesystem, close it, then publish with os.replace.
constraints: Purpose is design; no efficacy experiment or performance claim.
Two-candidate exception: the requirements explicitly limit the decision to these two real mechanisms; additional methods would expand the question.
Use only the fixture requirements and decisive Python os.replace and Linux rename(2) primary passages.

002-evidence-A.question: Truncate the checkpoint destination and write JSON directly; conditionally reasonable when interrupted-update checkpoint loss is acceptable and fewer lifecycle steps are preferred.

config.brief: Answer the narrow checkpoint design question in requirements.md with a conditional source-grounded conclusion, no experiment required. Read only decisive Python os.replace and Linux rename(2) primary passages. Explain atomicity vs durability, same-filesystem constraints. Two-candidate exception is appropriate. Complete the explanation and independent review.

plan.reason: Design plan frozen. Requirements and evaluation contract read; Python os.replace passage verified. Linux rename(2) retrieval failed through web access and curl DNS resolution; its decisive passages remain a required evidence gap before completion.
plan.goal: Compare two mechanisms for a single-process JSON checkpoint and produce a conditional, source-grounded recommendation with independent review.
plan.baseline: A: directly truncate and rewrite the checkpoint file. B: write complete JSON to a temporary file on the destination filesystem, close it, then publish with os.replace.
constraints: Purpose is design; no efficacy experiment or performance claim.
Two-candidate exception: the requirements explicitly limit the decision to these two real mechanisms; additional methods would expand the question.
Use only the fixture requirements and decisive Python os.replace and Linux rename(2) primary passages.
Python evidence: https://docs.python.org/3/library/os.html#os.replace, decisive passage at lines 1833–1836 confirms atomic rename on success and possible cross-filesystem failure.
Linux evidence pending: https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/rename.2.html, DESCRIPTION replacement semantics and ERRORS EXDEV.
Do not treat atomic visibility as a power-loss durability guarantee; the named sources cannot establish a complete durability protocol.
No checks executed, files modified, packages installed, memory written, commits or deployments.
Examples are illustrative reasoning, not measured outcomes; retain retrieval failures and unknowns.

criteria.title: Conditional mechanism choice
criteria.acceptance: Compare A and B and condition the recommendation on preserving a complete checkpoint during interrupted updates versus accepting checkpoint loss for simpler writes. Explain both mechanisms without claiming measured effectiveness.

criteria.title: Atomic publication scope
criteria.acceptance: Ground successful replacement semantics in the decisive Python and Linux passages. Distinguish publication of a completed temporary file from atomicity of its preceding writes; explain that existing open descriptors can retain the old file.

criteria.title: Durability boundary
criteria.acceptance: Separate atomic pathname visibility from persistence after power loss or system crash. State that durability is unmeasured and a complete synchronization protocol is not established by these passages.

criteria.title: Filesystem constraint
criteria.acceptance: Verify Linux EXDEV and Python's cross-filesystem warning; require the temporary file on the destination filesystem, preferably in its directory. Do not present a cross-filesystem copy fallback as atomic replacement.

criteria.title: Independent evidence review
criteria.acceptance: An independent reviewer checks the final explanation against the original decisive passages and R1–R4, retaining unsupported claims and source gaps as unresolved. Completion requires the Linux source gap to be closed.

plan.complexity_baseline: A uses one destination write sequence. B adds temporary-file lifecycle and a replacement operation. Compare these structural costs qualitatively; no timing or reliability measurement.

proposal_design.question: For a single-process JSON checkpoint, when should complete temporary-file replacement be preferred over direct truncating rewrite?
proposal_design.scope: One writer, an existing complete checkpoint, a distinct temporary file and no subsequent mutation; frozen candidates A and B only. Design comparison with zero experiments.

This conditional design conclusion addresses a program saving JSON for later restart. It establishes neither measured reliability nor power-loss durability.","scope":"Two frozen mechanisms for one writer updating an existing complete JSON checkpoint. B uses a distinct temporary file on the destination mounted filesystem, completes and closes it before replacement, and performs no subsequent mutation. Only the decisive Python os.replace and 2021 Linux rename(2) original passages support the documented replacement guarantees.","takeaway":"B separates preparation from publication: successful replacement publishes the prepared file atomically, while the preceding writes remain separate. Python documents atomic renaming on success and possible cross-filesystem failure ([Python os.replace](https://docs.python.org/3/library/os.html#os.replace), registered S1). Linux documents atomic destination replacement and EXDEV across different mount points, even mounts of the same filesystem ([Linux rename(2) original](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/mkerrisk/man-pages/master/man2/rename.2), registered SUPP_LINUX_RAW). Neither passage establishes persistence after power loss; completing and closing a file does not establish a complete durability protocol.","walkthrough":"Concrete with/without example, illustrative and unmeasured: checkpoint.json initially contains {\"step\":10}; the next checkpoint is {\"step\":11}. Without temporary-file replacement, A truncates checkpoint.json and writes the new JSON into that same file. Interruption after truncation or after writing only {\"step\": can leave empty or incomplete JSON; this is reasoning from the specified mechanism, not an observed failure. With B, the writer prepares checkpoint.tmp beside checkpoint.json. While the temporary file is incomplete, the destination still refers to the old checkpoint under the stated scope. After complete writing and closure, os.replace(checkpoint.tmp, checkpoint.json) publishes the new file if replacement succeeds. Figure F1 compares these paths; F2 expands the publication boundary rather than repeating the overview. Placing the temporary file beside the destination addresses the mount constraint, but does not ensure success. A cross-filesystem copy fallback would be a different mechanism and cannot inherit this atomic replacement guarantee. The Linux descriptor sentence directly concerns open descriptors for the source oldpath; readers already holding the old destination retaining that file is an inference, not that sentence's explicit guarantee. This example and both figures are explanations, not executed traces.","glossary":"Checkpoint: saved program state used on restart. Truncation: reducing the destination to zero length before rewriting in candidate A. Preparation: writing and closing B's distinct temporary file. Publication: replacing the destination pathname with that prepared file. Atomic replacement: a successful indivisible pathname change; Linux describes no interval in which an existing destination pathname is missing. Durability: persistence after power loss or system crash, which remains unknown here. Mounted filesystem: the rename placement boundary; Linux reports EXDEV across different mount points.","limitations":"Tested scope: none. plan.reason: Design plan frozen. Requirements and evaluation contract read; Python os.replace passage verified. Linux rename(2) retrieval failed through web access and curl DNS resolution; its decisive passages remain a required evidence gap before completion.
plan.goal: Compare two mechanisms for a single-process JSON checkpoint and produce a conditional, source-grounded recommendation with independent review.
plan.baseline: A: directly truncate and rewrite the checkpoint file. B: write complete JSON to a temporary file on the destination filesystem, close it, then publish with os.replace.
constraints: Purpose is design; no efficacy experiment or performance claim.
Two-candidate exception: the requirements explicitly limit the decision to these two real mechanisms; additional methods would expand the question.
Use only the fixture requirements and decisive Python os.replace and Linux rename(2) primary passages.
Python evidence: https://docs.python.org/3/library/os.html#os.replace, decisive passage at lines 1833–1836 confirms atomic rename on success and possible cross-filesystem failure.
Linux evidence pending: https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/rename.2.html, DESCRIPTION replacement semantics and ERRORS EXDEV.
Do not treat atomic visibility as a power-loss durability guarantee; the named sources cannot establish a complete durability protocol.
No checks executed, files modified, packages installed, memory written, commits or deployments.
Examples are illustrative reasoning, not measured outcomes; retain retrieval failures and unknowns.

The dossier's pending-review statements are stale, but the three unavailable man7 access records remain genuine failures. No experiments or paired measurements exist.

checks.reason: The proposal explains A's direct truncating rewrite and B's complete temporary-file preparation followed by replacement. It conditionally prefers B when preserving a complete checkpoint during interrupted updates matters, and A when checkpoint loss is acceptable and fewer lifecycle steps are preferred. Python os.replace documents atomic renaming on success; indexed original Linux DESCRIPTION supports atomic destination replacement. Complete-checkpoint preservation is explicitly mechanism reasoning, not measured effectiveness. Durability and actual interruption outcomes remain unknown. EV-00011 remains a failed Linux retrieval receipt; indexed original reading does not convert it into successful transport or runtime evidence. No runtime checks were executed.

Python os.replace documents atomic renaming upon success. Linux rename(2) DESCRIPTION documents atomic replacement of an existing destination without a missing-path interval and unaffected source-file descriptors. Proposal claims C5 and B-C4 and the reader guide correctly condition complete-JSON publication on completed preparation and successful replacement, keep preceding writes separate, and label existing destination readers retaining the old file as inference. Linux passages were independently read through indexed original-page text after direct access failed. Saved Linux timeout receipts remain failures; this source-based pass establishes no runtime or durability result.

Claims C4, A-C4 and B-C5, the comparison and reader-guide limitations explicitly separate atomic pathname visibility from power-loss or system-crash persistence. They state that durability is unmeasured and closure plus replacement establishes no complete synchronization protocol. Independently read [Python os.replace](https://docs.python.org/3/library/os.html#os.replace) and indexed original [Linux rename(2) DESCRIPTION](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/rename.2.html): these passages describe successful rename atomicity and pathname access, without establishing crash persistence. The supplied results contain no experiments, metrics or experiment receipts. Actual source receipts EV-00018 and EV-00019 record Python retrieval success and Linux timeout respectively; the Linux failure remains preserved. No previous R3 issues were supplied.

Python os.replace documents possible failure across filesystems. Linux rename(2) EXDEV specifies different mounted filesystems, including separate mounts of the same filesystem. The proposal requires destination-mount placement, preferably the destination directory, makes success conditional, and does not claim an atomic cross-filesystem copy fallback. Linux EXDEV was independently read through indexed original-page text; direct access returned Internal Error. Saved timeout receipts remain unchanged.

Reviewed R1–R4 within R5's independent-review scope. The conditional recommendation compares both requested mechanisms and labels interruption examples as unmeasured reasoning. Python os.replace documents atomic renaming on success and possible cross-filesystem failure. The original Linux manual independently confirms atomic destination replacement, unaffected source descriptors and EXDEV across different mount points, including mounts of the same filesystem. The explanation correctly leaves power-loss durability unknown. EV-00026 records successful retrieval of that original Linux source, whose decisive passages were independently read here; EV-00027–EV-00029 remain unavailable and are not recast as successes. No runtime outcomes, measurements or empirical acceptance are asserted. No previous issue records were supplied in the named inputs.

checks.reason: The proposal explains A's direct truncating rewrite and B's complete temporary-file preparation followed by replacement. It conditionally prefers B when preserving a complete checkpoint during interrupted updates matters, and A when checkpoint loss is acceptable and fewer lifecycle steps are preferred. Python os.replace documents atomic renaming on success; indexed original Linux DESCRIPTION supports atomic destination replacement. Complete-checkpoint preservation is explicitly mechanism reasoning, not measured effectiveness. Durability and actual interruption outcomes remain unknown. EV-00011 remains a failed Linux retrieval receipt; indexed original reading does not convert it into successful transport or runtime evidence. No runtime checks were executed.

Python os.replace documents atomic renaming upon success. Linux rename(2) DESCRIPTION documents atomic replacement of an existing destination without a missing-path interval and unaffected source-file descriptors. Proposal claims C5 and B-C4 and the reader guide correctly condition complete-JSON publication on completed preparation and successful replacement, keep preceding writes separate, and label existing destination readers retaining the old file as inference. Linux passages were independently read through indexed original-page text after direct access failed. Saved Linux timeout receipts remain failures; this source-based pass establishes no runtime or durability result.

Claims C4, A-C4 and B-C5, the comparison and reader-guide limitations explicitly separate atomic pathname visibility from power-loss or system-crash persistence. They state that durability is unmeasured and closure plus replacement establishes no complete synchronization protocol. Independently read [Python os.replace](https://docs.python.org/3/library/os.html#os.replace) and indexed original [Linux rename(2) DESCRIPTION](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/rename.2.html): these passages describe successful rename atomicity and pathname access, without establishing crash persistence. The supplied results contain no experiments, metrics or experiment receipts. Actual source receipts EV-00018 and EV-00019 record Python retrieval success and Linux timeout respectively; the Linux failure remains preserved. No previous R3 issues were supplied.

Python os.replace documents possible failure across filesystems. Linux rename(2) EXDEV specifies different mounted filesystems, including separate mounts of the same filesystem. The proposal requires destination-mount placement, preferably the destination directory, makes success conditional, and does not claim an atomic cross-filesystem copy fallback. Linux EXDEV was independently read through indexed original-page text; direct access returned Internal Error. Saved timeout receipts remain unchanged.

Reviewed R1–R4 within R5's independent-review scope. The conditional recommendation compares both requested mechanisms and labels interruption examples as unmeasured reasoning. Python os.replace documents atomic renaming on success and possible cross-filesystem failure. The original Linux manual independently confirms atomic destination replacement, unaffected source descriptors and EXDEV across different mount points, including mounts of the same filesystem. The explanation correctly leaves power-loss durability unknown. EV-00026 records successful retrieval of that original Linux source, whose decisive passages were independently read here; EV-00027–EV-00029 remain unavailable and are not recast as successes. No runtime outcomes, measurements or empirical acceptance are asserted. No previous issue records were supplied in the named inputs.

Examples are illustrative reasoning, not measured outcomes; retain retrieval failures and unknowns.

checks.reason: The proposal explains A's direct truncating rewrite and B's complete temporary-file preparation followed by replacement. It conditionally prefers B when preserving a complete checkpoint during interrupted updates matters, and A when checkpoint loss is acceptable and fewer lifecycle steps are preferred. Python os.replace documents atomic renaming on success; indexed original Linux DESCRIPTION supports atomic destination replacement. Complete-checkpoint preservation is explicitly mechanism reasoning, not measured effectiveness. Durability and actual interruption outcomes remain unknown. EV-00011 remains a failed Linux retrieval receipt; indexed original reading does not convert it into successful transport or runtime evidence. No runtime checks were executed.

Python os.replace documents atomic renaming upon success. Linux rename(2) DESCRIPTION documents atomic replacement of an existing destination without a missing-path interval and unaffected source-file descriptors. Proposal claims C5 and B-C4 and the reader guide correctly condition complete-JSON publication on completed preparation and successful replacement, keep preceding writes separate, and label existing destination readers retaining the old file as inference. Linux passages were independently read through indexed original-page text after direct access failed. Saved Linux timeout receipts remain failures; this source-based pass establishes no runtime or durability result.

Claims C4, A-C4 and B-C5, the comparison and reader-guide limitations explicitly separate atomic pathname visibility from power-loss or system-crash persistence. They state that durability is unmeasured and closure plus replacement establishes no complete synchronization protocol. Independently read [Python os.replace](https://docs.python.org/3/library/os.html#os.replace) and indexed original [Linux rename(2) DESCRIPTION](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/rename.2.html): these passages describe successful rename atomicity and pathname access, without establishing crash persistence. The supplied results contain no experiments, metrics or experiment receipts. Actual source receipts EV-00018 and EV-00019 record Python retrieval success and Linux timeout respectively; the Linux failure remains preserved. No previous R3 issues were supplied.

Python os.replace documents possible failure across filesystems. Linux rename(2) EXDEV specifies different mounted filesystems, including separate mounts of the same filesystem. The proposal requires destination-mount placement, preferably the destination directory, makes success conditional, and does not claim an atomic cross-filesystem copy fallback. Linux EXDEV was independently read through indexed original-page text; direct access returned Internal Error. Saved timeout receipts remain unchanged.

Reviewed R1–R4 within R5's independent-review scope. The conditional recommendation compares both requested mechanisms and labels interruption examples as unmeasured reasoning. Python os.replace documents atomic renaming on success and possible cross-filesystem failure. The original Linux manual independently confirms atomic destination replacement, unaffected source descriptors and EXDEV across different mount points, including mounts of the same filesystem. The explanation correctly leaves power-loss durability unknown. EV-00026 records successful retrieval of that original Linux source, whose decisive passages were independently read here; EV-00027–EV-00029 remain unavailable and are not recast as successes. No runtime outcomes, measurements or empirical acceptance are asserted. No previous issue records were supplied in the named inputs.

plan.complexity_baseline: A uses one destination write sequence. B adds temporary-file lifecycle and a replacement operation. Compare these structural costs qualitatively; no timing or reliability measurement.

checks.reason: The proposal explains A's direct truncating rewrite and B's complete temporary-file preparation followed by replacement. It conditionally prefers B when preserving a complete checkpoint during interrupted updates matters, and A when checkpoint loss is acceptable and fewer lifecycle steps are preferred. Python os.replace documents atomic renaming on success; indexed original Linux DESCRIPTION supports atomic destination replacement. Complete-checkpoint preservation is explicitly mechanism reasoning, not measured effectiveness. Durability and actual interruption outcomes remain unknown. EV-00011 remains a failed Linux retrieval receipt; indexed original reading does not convert it into successful transport or runtime evidence. No runtime checks were executed.

Python os.replace documents atomic renaming upon success. Linux rename(2) DESCRIPTION documents atomic replacement of an existing destination without a missing-path interval and unaffected source-file descriptors. Proposal claims C5 and B-C4 and the reader guide correctly condition complete-JSON publication on completed preparation and successful replacement, keep preceding writes separate, and label existing destination readers retaining the old file as inference. Linux passages were independently read through indexed original-page text after direct access failed. Saved Linux timeout receipts remain failures; this source-based pass establishes no runtime or durability result.

checks.reason: [Python os.replace](https://docs.python.org/3/library/os.html#os.replace) warns that replacement may fail across filesystems. The [Linux rename(2) original](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/mkerrisk/man-pages/master/man2/rename.2), EXDEV lines 426–432, requires the same mounted filesystem and excludes different mount points even when both mount the same filesystem. The current proposal requires destination-mount placement, preferably beside the checkpoint, conditions publication on successful replacement, and explicitly denies an atomic cross-filesystem copy fallback. Saved man7 timeouts remain failures; the successfully retrieved 2021 original does not verify the unavailable newer page. This is a design pass, not runtime validation.

checks.reason: The proposal explains A's direct truncating rewrite and B's complete temporary-file preparation followed by replacement. It conditionally prefers B when preserving a complete checkpoint during interrupted updates matters, and A when checkpoint loss is acceptable and fewer lifecycle steps are preferred. Python os.replace documents atomic renaming on success; indexed original Linux DESCRIPTION supports atomic destination replacement. Complete-checkpoint preservation is explicitly mechanism reasoning, not measured effectiveness. Durability and actual interruption outcomes remain unknown. EV-00011 remains a failed Linux retrieval receipt; indexed original reading does not convert it into successful transport or runtime evidence. No runtime checks were executed.

Python os.replace documents atomic renaming upon success. Linux rename(2) DESCRIPTION documents atomic replacement of an existing destination without a missing-path interval and unaffected source-file descriptors. Proposal claims C5 and B-C4 and the reader guide correctly condition complete-JSON publication on completed preparation and successful replacement, keep preceding writes separate, and label existing destination readers retaining the old file as inference. Linux passages were independently read through indexed original-page text after direct access failed. Saved Linux timeout receipts remain failures; this source-based pass establishes no runtime or durability result.

Claims C4, A-C4 and B-C5, the comparison and reader-guide limitations explicitly separate atomic pathname visibility from power-loss or system-crash persistence. They state that durability is unmeasured and closure plus replacement establishes no complete synchronization protocol. Independently read [Python os.replace](https://docs.python.org/3/library/os.html#os.replace) and indexed original [Linux rename(2) DESCRIPTION](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/rename.2.html): these passages describe successful rename atomicity and pathname access, without establishing crash persistence. The supplied results contain no experiments, metrics or experiment receipts. Actual source receipts EV-00018 and EV-00019 record Python retrieval success and Linux timeout respectively; the Linux failure remains preserved. No previous R3 issues were supplied.

Python os.replace documents possible failure across filesystems. Linux rename(2) EXDEV specifies different mounted filesystems, including separate mounts of the same filesystem. The proposal requires destination-mount placement, preferably the destination directory, makes success conditional, and does not claim an atomic cross-filesystem copy fallback. Linux EXDEV was independently read through indexed original-page text; direct access returned Internal Error. Saved timeout receipts remain unchanged.

Reviewed R1–R4 within R5's independent-review scope. The conditional recommendation compares both requested mechanisms and labels interruption examples as unmeasured reasoning. Python os.replace documents atomic renaming on success and possible cross-filesystem failure. The original Linux manual independently confirms atomic destination replacement, unaffected source descriptors and EXDEV across different mount points, including mounts of the same filesystem. The explanation correctly leaves power-loss durability unknown. EV-00026 records successful retrieval of that original Linux source, whose decisive passages were independently read here; EV-00027–EV-00029 remain unavailable and are not recast as successes. No runtime outcomes, measurements or empirical acceptance are asserted. No previous issue records were supplied in the named inputs.

checks.reason: Independently reviewed the current proposal against R1–R4. It compares both requested mechanisms and conditions preference for B on complete preparation and successful replacement. [Python os.replace](https://docs.python.org/3/library/os.html#os.replace) supports successful-rename atomicity and possible cross-filesystem failure. The [2021 Linux original](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/mkerrisk/man-pages/master/man2/rename.2), DESCRIPTION lines 66–105 and EXDEV lines 426–432, supports atomic destination replacement, unaffected source descriptors, and the mount boundary. Actual receipts EV-00046 and EV-00047 record successful original-source retrieval, closing the decisive-passage gap within that dated scope. EV-00040–EV-00045 remain failed man7 retrievals; the unavailable newer version is not verified. The proposal labels truncation interruption behavior and destination-reader behavior as reasoning, leaves crash durability unknown, and treats earlier review grades as applying only to the earlier proposal. No previous R5 issues were supplied. No experiments or runtime passes are asserted; parent provenance assessment remains pending.

config.brief: Answer the narrow checkpoint design question in requirements.md with a conditional source-grounded conclusion, no experiment required. Read only decisive Python os.replace and Linux rename(2) primary passages. Explain atomicity vs durability, same-filesystem constraints. Two-candidate exception is appropriate. Complete the explanation and independent review.

plan.reason: Design plan frozen. Requirements and evaluation contract read; Python os.replace passage verified. Linux rename(2) retrieval failed through web access and curl DNS resolution; its decisive passages remain a required evidence gap before completion.
plan.goal: Compare two mechanisms for a single-process JSON checkpoint and produce a conditional, source-grounded recommendation with independent review.
plan.baseline: A: directly truncate and rewrite the checkpoint file. B: write complete JSON to a temporary file on the destination filesystem, close it, then publish with os.replace.
constraints: Purpose is design; no efficacy experiment or performance claim.
Two-candidate exception: the requirements explicitly limit the decision to these two real mechanisms; additional methods would expand the question.
Use only the fixture requirements and decisive Python os.replace and Linux rename(2) primary passages.
Python evidence: https://docs.python.org/3/library/os.html#os.replace, decisive passage at lines 1833–1836 confirms atomic rename on success and possible cross-filesystem failure.
Linux evidence pending: https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/rename.2.html, DESCRIPTION replacement semantics and ERRORS EXDEV.
Do not treat atomic visibility as a power-loss durability guarantee; the named sources cannot establish a complete durability protocol.
No checks executed, files modified, packages installed, memory written, commits or deployments.
Examples are illustrative reasoning, not measured outcomes; retain retrieval failures and unknowns.

criteria.title: Conditional mechanism choice
criteria.acceptance: Compare A and B and condition the recommendation on preserving a complete checkpoint during interrupted updates versus accepting checkpoint loss for simpler writes. Explain both mechanisms without claiming measured effectiveness.

criteria.title: Atomic publication scope
criteria.acceptance: Ground successful replacement semantics in the decisive Python and Linux passages. Distinguish publication of a completed temporary file from atomicity of its preceding writes; explain that existing open descriptors can retain the old file.

criteria.title: Durability boundary
criteria.acceptance: Separate atomic pathname visibility from persistence after power loss or system crash. State that durability is unmeasured and a complete synchronization protocol is not established by these passages.

criteria.title: Filesystem constraint
criteria.acceptance: Verify Linux EXDEV and Python's cross-filesystem warning; require the temporary file on the destination filesystem, preferably in its directory. Do not present a cross-filesystem copy fallback as atomic replacement.

criteria.title: Independent evidence review
criteria.acceptance: An independent reviewer checks the final explanation against the original decisive passages and R1–R4, retaining unsupported claims and source gaps as unresolved. Completion requires the Linux source gap to be closed.

plan.complexity_baseline: A uses one destination write sequence. B adds temporary-file lifecycle and a replacement operation. Compare these structural costs qualitatively; no timing or reliability measurement.

checks.reason: The proposal explains A's direct truncating rewrite and B's complete temporary-file preparation followed by replacement. It conditionally prefers B when preserving a complete checkpoint during interrupted updates matters, and A when checkpoint loss is acceptable and fewer lifecycle steps are preferred. Python os.replace documents atomic renaming on success; indexed original Linux DESCRIPTION supports atomic destination replacement. Complete-checkpoint preservation is explicitly mechanism reasoning, not measured effectiveness. Durability and actual interruption outcomes remain unknown. EV-00011 remains a failed Linux retrieval receipt; indexed original reading does not convert it into successful transport or runtime evidence. No runtime checks were executed.

Python os.replace documents atomic renaming upon success. Linux rename(2) DESCRIPTION documents atomic replacement of an existing destination without a missing-path interval and unaffected source-file descriptors. Proposal claims C5 and B-C4 and the reader guide correctly condition complete-JSON publication on completed preparation and successful replacement, keep preceding writes separate, and label existing destination readers retaining the old file as inference. Linux passages were independently read through indexed original-page text after direct access failed. Saved Linux timeout receipts remain failures; this source-based pass establishes no runtime or durability result.

Claims C4, A-C4 and B-C5, the comparison and reader-guide limitations explicitly separate atomic pathname visibility from power-loss or system-crash persistence. They state that durability is unmeasured and closure plus replacement establishes no complete synchronization protocol. Independently read [Python os.replace](https://docs.python.org/3/library/os.html#os.replace) and indexed original [Linux rename(2) DESCRIPTION](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/rename.2.html): these passages describe successful rename atomicity and pathname access, without establishing crash persistence. The supplied results contain no experiments, metrics or experiment receipts. Actual source receipts EV-00018 and EV-00019 record Python retrieval success and Linux timeout respectively; the Linux failure remains preserved. No previous R3 issues were supplied.

Python os.replace documents possible failure across filesystems. Linux rename(2) EXDEV specifies different mounted filesystems, including separate mounts of the same filesystem. The proposal requires destination-mount placement, preferably the destination directory, makes success conditional, and does not claim an atomic cross-filesystem copy fallback. Linux EXDEV was independently read through indexed original-page text; direct access returned Internal Error. Saved timeout receipts remain unchanged.

Reviewed R1–R4 within R5's independent-review scope. The conditional recommendation compares both requested mechanisms and labels interruption examples as unmeasured reasoning. Python os.replace documents atomic renaming on success and possible cross-filesystem failure. The original Linux manual independently confirms atomic destination replacement, unaffected source descriptors and EXDEV across different mount points, including mounts of the same filesystem. The explanation correctly leaves power-loss durability unknown. EV-00026 records successful retrieval of that original Linux source, whose decisive passages were independently read here; EV-00027–EV-00029 remain unavailable and are not recast as successes. No runtime outcomes, measurements or empirical acceptance are asserted. No previous issue records were supplied in the named inputs.

checks.reason: The saved proposal explains A's truncation followed by direct writing and B's complete, distinct temporary-file preparation followed by replacement. It prefers B when preserving complete checkpoint publication during interrupted updates matters, conditional on completed preparation and successful replacement on the destination mount. It permits A when interrupted-update checkpoint loss is acceptable and fewer lifecycle steps are preferred. Independently read Python os.replace and original Linux rename(2) passages support successful replacement atomicity. A's partial-write risk and B's checkpoint preservation are explicitly mechanism reasoning; examples and figures are unmeasured. Crash durability remains unknown. Actual receipts EV-00001 and EV-00026 record source retrieval, while EV-00042 remains a timeout failure. No experiments or runtime receipts exist. No previous R1 issues were supplied.

criterion_reviews.complexity_reason: The authorized two-candidate exception fits the narrow question. B adds temporary-file lifecycle and replacement to A's direct write sequence; the proposal explains these structural costs qualitatively without claiming measured latency or reliability. No additional mechanism or experiment is required for R1.

checks.reason: [Python os.replace](https://docs.python.org/3/library/os.html#os.replace) documents atomic renaming upon success. The [2021 Linux rename(2) original](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/mkerrisk/man-pages/master/man2/rename.2) documents atomic replacement of an existing destination without a missing-path interval and unaffected oldpath descriptors. Current claims C5 and B-C3 and the reader guide correctly separate completed temporary-file preparation from successful atomic publication. Existing destination readers retaining old file references is explicitly labeled inference, rather than attributed to the source-descriptor sentence. Successful Linux transport receipts support source availability; saved man7 timeouts remain failures. This qualitative pass establishes no runtime, interruption, or durability result.

criterion_reviews.complexity_reason: The review stays within R2 and the two specified mechanisms. Separating preparation, pathname publication, and retained reader references adds necessary explanatory detail without adding experiments or implementation scope. Lifecycle costs remain qualitative and unmeasured.

checks.reason: Claims C4, A-C4 and B-C5, the durability comparison, decision and reader-guide limitations explicitly distinguish atomic pathname visibility from persistence after power loss or system crash. They retain durability as unknown and unmeasured and state that closing the temporary file and replacing the destination establish no complete synchronization protocol. Independently read [Python os.replace](https://docs.python.org/3/library/os.html#os.replace) and [Linux rename(2) original DESCRIPTION](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/mkerrisk/man-pages/master/man2/rename.2): these passages describe successful rename atomicity and pathname access, without establishing crash persistence. Actual iteration 2 Linux receipts EV-00046 and EV-00047 record successful source retrieval; EV-00044 remains a failed man7 retrieval. The saved results contain no experiments, metrics or experiment receipts; illustrations are explicitly unmeasured. This is a qualitative design pass, not runtime or durability verification. No previous R3 issues were supplied.

criterion_reviews.complexity_reason: The durability explanation stays within the two requested mechanisms. It identifies B's additional temporary-file lifecycle and replacement steps qualitatively, without introducing an unsupported synchronization protocol or measured performance claim. The explicit two-candidate exception is appropriate for this narrow design question.

checks.reason: [Python os.replace](https://docs.python.org/3/library/os.html#os.replace) warns that replacement may fail across filesystems. The [Linux rename(2) original](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/mkerrisk/man-pages/master/man2/rename.2), EXDEV lines 426–432, requires the same mounted filesystem and excludes different mount points even when both mount the same filesystem. The current proposal requires destination-mount placement, preferably beside the checkpoint, conditions publication on successful replacement, and explicitly denies an atomic cross-filesystem copy fallback. Saved man7 timeouts remain failures; the successfully retrieved 2021 original does not verify the unavailable newer page. This is a design pass, not runtime validation.

criterion_reviews.complexity_reason: Destination-directory placement satisfies the documented mount constraint within candidate B's existing temporary-file lifecycle. The proposal adds no copy fallback or additional mechanism. Structural costs remain qualitative; no performance or reliability measurements are claimed.

checks.reason: Independently reviewed the current proposal against R1–R4. It compares both requested mechanisms and conditions preference for B on complete preparation and successful replacement. [Python os.replace](https://docs.python.org/3/library/os.html#os.replace) supports successful-rename atomicity and possible cross-filesystem failure. The [2021 Linux original](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/mkerrisk/man-pages/master/man2/rename.2), DESCRIPTION lines 66–105 and EXDEV lines 426–432, supports atomic destination replacement, unaffected source descriptors, and the mount boundary. Actual receipts EV-00046 and EV-00047 record successful original-source retrieval, closing the decisive-passage gap within that dated scope. EV-00040–EV-00045 remain failed man7 retrievals; the unavailable newer version is not verified. The proposal labels truncation interruption behavior and destination-reader behavior as reasoning, leaves crash durability unknown, and treats earlier review grades as applying only to the earlier proposal. No previous R5 issues were supplied. No experiments or runtime passes are asserted; parent provenance assessment remains pending.

criteria.title: Conditional mechanism choice
criteria.acceptance: Compare A and B and condition the recommendation on preserving a complete checkpoint during interrupted updates versus accepting checkpoint loss for simpler writes. Explain both mechanisms without claiming measured effectiveness.

criteria.title: Atomic publication scope
criteria.acceptance: Ground successful replacement semantics in the decisive Python and Linux passages. Distinguish publication of a completed temporary file from atomicity of its preceding writes; explain that existing open descriptors can retain the old file.

criteria.title: Durability boundary
criteria.acceptance: Separate atomic pathname visibility from persistence after power loss or system crash. State that durability is unmeasured and a complete synchronization protocol is not established by these passages.

criteria.title: Filesystem constraint
criteria.acceptance: Verify Linux EXDEV and Python's cross-filesystem warning; require the temporary file on the destination filesystem, preferably in its directory. Do not present a cross-filesystem copy fallback as atomic replacement.

criteria.title: Independent evidence review
criteria.acceptance: An independent reviewer checks the final explanation against the original decisive passages and R1–R4, retaining unsupported claims and source gaps as unresolved. Completion requires the Linux source gap to be closed.

reader_guide.purpose: Prefer B, complete temporary-file replacement, when publishing a complete checkpoint matters; prefer A, direct truncating rewrite, only when interrupted-update checkpoint loss is acceptable and fewer lifecycle steps are preferred. This conditional design conclusion addresses a program saving JSON for later restart. Independent qualitative review of the current explanation passed R1–R5; reliability and power-loss durability remain unmeasured.
reader_guide.scope: Two frozen mechanisms for one writer updating an existing complete JSON checkpoint. B uses a distinct temporary file on the destination mounted filesystem, completes and closes it before replacement, and performs no subsequent mutation. Only the decisive Python os.replace and 2021 Linux rename(2) original passages support the documented replacement guarantees.
reader_guide.takeaway: B separates preparation from publication: successful replacement publishes the prepared file atomically, while the preceding writes remain separate. Python documents atomic renaming on success and possible cross-filesystem failure ([Python os.replace](https://docs.python.org/3/library/os.html#os.replace), registered S1). Linux documents atomic destination replacement and EXDEV across different mount points, even mounts of the same filesystem ([Linux rename(2) original](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/mkerrisk/man-pages/master/man2/rename.2), registered SUPP_LINUX_RAW). Neither passage establishes persistence after power loss; completing and closing a file does not establish a complete durability protocol.
reader_guide.walkthrough: Concrete with/without example, illustrative and unmeasured: checkpoint.json initially contains {"step":10}; the next checkpoint is {"step":11}. Without temporary-file replacement, A truncates checkpoint.json and writes the new JSON into that same file. Interruption after truncation or after writing only {"step": can leave empty or incomplete JSON; this is reasoning from the specified mechanism, not an observed failure. With B, the writer prepares checkpoint.tmp beside checkpoint.json. While the temporary file is incomplete, the destination still refers to the old checkpoint under the stated scope. After complete writing and closure, os.replace(checkpoint.tmp, checkpoint.json) publishes the new file if replacement succeeds. Figure F1 compares these paths; F2 expands the publication boundary rather than repeating the overview. Placing the temporary file beside the destination addresses the mount constraint, but does not ensure success. A cross-filesystem copy fallback would be a different mechanism and cannot inherit this atomic replacement guarantee. The Linux descriptor sentence directly concerns open descriptors for the source oldpath; readers already holding the old destination retaining that file is an inference, not that sentence's explicit guarantee. This example and both figures are explanations, not executed traces.
reader_guide.glossary: Checkpoint: saved program state used on restart. Truncation: reducing the destination to zero length before rewriting in candidate A. Preparation: writing and closing B's distinct temporary file. Publication: replacing the destination pathname with that prepared file. Atomic replacement: a successful indivisible pathname change; Linux describes no interval in which an existing destination pathname is missing. Durability: persistence after power loss or system crash, which remains unknown here. Mounted filesystem: the rename placement boundary; Linux reports EXDEV across different mount points.
reader_guide.limitations: Tested scope: none. There are zero experimental tasks, paired trials, metrics, successful experiment receipts or exported paired-result JSON. No latency, interrupted-update outcomes, failure frequencies or filesystem-specific crash durability were measured. Current independent qualitative review is complete, with R1–R5 passing; these grades establish review of the explanation, not empirical effectiveness or human acceptance. Parent provenance assessment remains unresolved. Registered man7 retrieval timeouts remain failures; earlier narrative also records Internal Error and DNS failures. Successful retrieval of the separately registered 2021 original closes decisive-passage support within that dated scope and does not verify the unavailable newer page. Transport receipts establish access, not mechanism efficacy. Figure rendering and reader understanding were not tested.
reader_guide.comparison_exception: The frozen target is five methods, but the requirements expressly ask for A, direct truncating rewrite, and B, complete same-filesystem temporary-file replacement. Adding three alternatives would expand the narrow checkpoint decision rather than improve its requested comparison.

checks.reason: The proposal explains A's direct truncating rewrite and B's complete temporary-file preparation followed by replacement. It conditionally prefers B when preserving a complete checkpoint during interrupted updates matters, and A when checkpoint loss is acceptable and fewer lifecycle steps are preferred. Python os.replace documents atomic renaming on success; indexed original Linux DESCRIPTION supports atomic destination replacement. Complete-checkpoint preservation is explicitly mechanism reasoning, not measured effectiveness. Durability and actual interruption outcomes remain unknown. EV-00011 remains a failed Linux retrieval receipt; indexed original reading does not convert it into successful transport or runtime evidence. No runtime checks were executed.

Python os.replace documents atomic renaming upon success. Linux rename(2) DESCRIPTION documents atomic replacement of an existing destination without a missing-path interval and unaffected source-file descriptors. Proposal claims C5 and B-C4 and the reader guide correctly condition complete-JSON publication on completed preparation and successful replacement, keep preceding writes separate, and label existing destination readers retaining the old file as inference. Linux passages were independently read through indexed original-page text after direct access failed. Saved Linux timeout receipts remain failures; this source-based pass establishes no runtime or durability result.

Claims C4, A-C4 and B-C5, the comparison and reader-guide limitations explicitly separate atomic pathname visibility from power-loss or system-crash persistence. They state that durability is unmeasured and closure plus replacement establishes no complete synchronization protocol. Independently read [Python os.replace](https://docs.python.org/3/library/os.html#os.replace) and indexed original [Linux rename(2) DESCRIPTION](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/rename.2.html): these passages describe successful rename atomicity and pathname access, without establishing crash persistence. The supplied results contain no experiments, metrics or experiment receipts. Actual source receipts EV-00018 and EV-00019 record Python retrieval success and Linux timeout respectively; the Linux failure remains preserved. No previous R3 issues were supplied.

Python os.replace documents possible failure across filesystems. Linux rename(2) EXDEV specifies different mounted filesystems, including separate mounts of the same filesystem. The proposal requires destination-mount placement, preferably the destination directory, makes success conditional, and does not claim an atomic cross-filesystem copy fallback. Linux EXDEV was independently read through indexed original-page text; direct access returned Internal Error. Saved timeout receipts remain unchanged.

Reviewed R1–R4 within R5's independent-review scope. The conditional recommendation compares both requested mechanisms and labels interruption examples as unmeasured reasoning. Python os.replace documents atomic renaming on success and possible cross-filesystem failure. The original Linux manual independently confirms atomic destination replacement, unaffected source descriptors and EXDEV across different mount points, including mounts of the same filesystem. The explanation correctly leaves power-loss durability unknown. EV-00026 records successful retrieval of that original Linux source, whose decisive passages were independently read here; EV-00027–EV-00029 remain unavailable and are not recast as successes. No runtime outcomes, measurements or empirical acceptance are asserted. No previous issue records were supplied in the named inputs.

checks.reason: The saved proposal explains A's truncation followed by direct writing and B's complete, distinct temporary-file preparation followed by replacement. It prefers B when preserving complete checkpoint publication during interrupted updates matters, conditional on completed preparation and successful replacement on the destination mount. It permits A when interrupted-update checkpoint loss is acceptable and fewer lifecycle steps are preferred. Independently read Python os.replace and original Linux rename(2) passages support successful replacement atomicity. A's partial-write risk and B's checkpoint preservation are explicitly mechanism reasoning; examples and figures are unmeasured. Crash durability remains unknown. Actual receipts EV-00001 and EV-00026 record source retrieval, while EV-00042 remains a timeout failure. No experiments or runtime receipts exist. No previous R1 issues were supplied.

[Python os.replace](https://docs.python.org/3/library/os.html#os.replace) documents atomic renaming upon success. The [2021 Linux rename(2) original](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/mkerrisk/man-pages/master/man2/rename.2) documents atomic replacement of an existing destination without a missing-path interval and unaffected oldpath descriptors. Current claims C5 and B-C3 and the reader guide correctly separate completed temporary-file preparation from successful atomic publication. Existing destination readers retaining old file references is explicitly labeled inference, rather than attributed to the source-descriptor sentence. Successful Linux transport receipts support source availability; saved man7 timeouts remain failures. This qualitative pass establishes no runtime, interruption, or durability result.

Claims C4, A-C4 and B-C5, the durability comparison, decision and reader-guide limitations explicitly distinguish atomic pathname visibility from persistence after power loss or system crash. They retain durability as unknown and unmeasured and state that closing the temporary file and replacing the destination establish no complete synchronization protocol. Independently read [Python os.replace](https://docs.python.org/3/library/os.html#os.replace) and [Linux rename(2) original DESCRIPTION](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/mkerrisk/man-pages/master/man2/rename.2): these passages describe successful rename atomicity and pathname access, without establishing crash persistence. Actual iteration 2 Linux receipts EV-00046 and EV-00047 record successful source retrieval; EV-00044 remains a failed man7 retrieval. The saved results contain no experiments, metrics or experiment receipts; illustrations are explicitly unmeasured. This is a qualitative design pass, not runtime or durability verification. No previous R3 issues were supplied.

[Python os.replace](https://docs.python.org/3/library/os.html#os.replace) warns that replacement may fail across filesystems. The [Linux rename(2) original](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/mkerrisk/man-pages/master/man2/rename.2), EXDEV lines 426–432, requires the same mounted filesystem and excludes different mount points even when both mount the same filesystem. The current proposal requires destination-mount placement, preferably beside the checkpoint, conditions publication on successful replacement, and explicitly denies an atomic cross-filesystem copy fallback. Saved man7 timeouts remain failures; the successfully retrieved 2021 original does not verify the unavailable newer page. This is a design pass, not runtime validation.

Independently reviewed the current proposal against R1–R4. It compares both requested mechanisms and conditions preference for B on complete preparation and successful replacement. [Python os.replace](https://docs.python.org/3/library/os.html#os.replace) supports successful-rename atomicity and possible cross-filesystem failure. The [2021 Linux original](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/mkerrisk/man-pages/master/man2/rename.2), DESCRIPTION lines 66–105 and EXDEV lines 426–432, supports atomic destination replacement, unaffected source descriptors, and the mount boundary. Actual receipts EV-00046 and EV-00047 record successful original-source retrieval, closing the decisive-passage gap within that dated scope. EV-00040–EV-00045 remain failed man7 retrievals; the unavailable newer version is not verified. The proposal labels truncation interruption behavior and destination-reader behavior as reasoning, leaves crash durability unknown, and treats earlier review grades as applying only to the earlier proposal. No previous R5 issues were supplied. No experiments or runtime passes are asserted; parent provenance assessment remains pending.
